quotes.text: Mapping catalogs what you have and where it sits. Assessment, on the other hand, asks whether those files still matter, who actually touches them, and how they fit into business workflows.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Draws a clear line between content mapping and content assessment.

quotes.text: Neat diagrams don't always point to value. A perfectly labeled collection of inactive files is still clutter, just with tidy labels.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Pithy warning against equating tidy structure with useful content.

quotes.text: A file isn't valuable because it exists. It's valuable because it's used when someone needs it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Argues for usage-based rather than volume-based content reporting.

quotes.text: The gap isn't the absence of content, it's the disconnect between user intent and system design that's the foundation of ongoing complaints about findability.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Pinpoints the root cause of findability problems.

quotes.text: You stop treating frustration as noise and start treating it as diagnostic data. Every abandoned search, duplicate file, or repeated query is a marker showing where the system is out of sync.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes user workarounds as actionable evidence.

takeaways: A tidy SharePoint content map shows where files should live, not whether anyone finds or uses them.
A real assessment combines structural, behavioral and contextual evidence, using usage reports and search logs to separate active content from clutter.
Turn findings into a report with quick wins, medium-term projects, long-term governance commitments and named owners with KPIs.
hook: Your SharePoint structure may look perfect on paper while users still cannot find what they need. This episode gives Microsoft 365 admins and information managers a three-layer method to audit structure, usage and value, and to turn the results into a findability roadmap leadership will act on.
